title: Linear programming: feasible regions and tied optima
attribution: Original questions, distractors, worked examples and interface prepared for RecallWeave with AI assistance. Mathematical background: MIT 6.854, Linear Programming notes, https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.854/21/Notes/n11-lp.html. No reference exercises, diagrams or passages are reproduced.
license: Original course content for the Jacob-Met/RecallWeave project; no additional reuse license is granted here. Linked references retain their own terms.

items.prompt: A problem requires 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 4, x+y ≤ 4 and 2x+y ≤ 5. Is (1,2) feasible?
options: Yes: it satisfies the rectangle and both authored inequalities.
Yes: being inside the rectangle is sufficient.
No: every feasible point must make an inequality an equality.
No: only rectangle corners can be feasible.
items.explanation: At (1,2), x+y=3 ≤ 4 and 2x+y=4 ≤ 5. Both coordinates also lie between 0 and 4. Feasibility requires every condition, but none has to be tight.
items.transfer: Check (2,2). Which single authored inequality excludes it?

items.prompt: For 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 4, x+y ≤ 4 and 2x+y ≤ 5, the rectangle boundaries x=4 and y=4 intersect at (4,4). What does this establish?
options: It is automatically a maximizing vertex.
Every boundary intersection is feasible.
It is a candidate intersection, but fails both authored inequalities.
One failed intersection proves the entire feasible set is empty.
items.explanation: The crossing supplies a candidate, not a feasibility certificate. At (4,4), the authored left sides are 8 and 12, exceeding 4 and 5. Other intersections can still be feasible.
items.transfer: Test the crossing of x=0 and x+y=4 against all constraints.

items.prompt: What is the exact intersection of 2x+y=5 and x+2y=5?
items.explanation: Subtracting the equations gives x-y=0. Substituting x=y gives 3x=5, so x=y=5/3. These fractional coordinates are valid for real variables.
items.transfer: Substitute 5/3 into both equations without rounding.

items.prompt: A feasible polygon has vertices (0,0), (0,4), (1,3) and (5/2,0). What is the maximum of 3x+2y?
items.explanation: The four exact values are 0, 8, 9 and 15/2. The largest is 9. A nonempty bounded polytope has a vertex attaining a linear optimum; here only one vertex attains 9.
items.transfer: How would the four values change if the objective were x-y?

items.prompt: Within 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 4, require 2x+y ≤ 5 and x+2y ≤ 5. What is the maximum of x+y over real variables?
options: 3, obtained by rounding the intersection down
5, because both right sides are 5
items.explanation: Adding the inequalities gives 3(x+y) ≤ 10. The point (5/3,5/3) meets both with equality and lies in the rectangle, so it attains the bound 10/3. No rounding is part of this continuous problem.
items.transfer: Explain why (2,2) violates both authored inequalities.

items.prompt: The vertices are (0,0), (0,4), (1,3) and (5/2,0). What is the minimum of 3x+2y?
options: A minimum cannot exist with real variables.
items.explanation: The exact vertex values are 0, 8, 9 and 15/2, so the minimum is 0 at the origin. This feasible set is nonempty and bounded.
items.transfer: Negate the objective and identify its maximum.

items.prompt: For x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 and x+y ≤ 4, maximize x+y. What is the complete optimal set?
options: Only the two points (0,4) and (4,0)
Every point of the feasible triangle
Only whichever maximizing vertex is listed first
The entire segment joining (0,4) and (4,0)
items.explanation: The upper bound is 4. Every point on the segment x+y=4 between the two intercepts attains it. Interior points below that edge have smaller values. Reporting endpoints alone must still explain the connecting optimal segment.

items.prompt: The feasible set is a nonempty triangle. What is the complete optimum set for 0x+0y?
options: Only the origin
Every feasible point, including the interior
Only the triangle's vertices
A zero objective is an invalid linear objective.
items.explanation: The objective equals 0 at every feasible point, so the whole triangle is optimal for either minimization or maximization. Vertices describe its boundary, not the only optimal points.
items.transfer: If the feasible set were a line segment instead, what would the complete optimal set be?

items.prompt: Require x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 and x+y ≤ -1. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The feasible set is empty, so there is no attained optimum.
The optimum is 0 at the origin.
The optimum must be -1 because it is the right side.
The problem is unbounded because no feasible vertex exists.
items.explanation: Nonnegative x and y have a nonnegative sum, which cannot be at most -1. No point satisfies all conditions. An empty feasible set has no attained optimum; that is different from an unbounded objective.
items.transfer: Replace -1 by 0 and describe the feasible set.

items.prompt: In 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 4, impose x+y ≤ 3 and -x-y ≤ -3. Minimize 2x+2y. What is the complete optimal set?
options: A polygon with positive area
Only (0,3)
The entire feasible segment x+y=3, with value 6
No complete set can be optimal when the objective coefficients are nonzero.
items.explanation: Together the inequalities require x+y=3. In the rectangle this is the segment from (0,3) to (3,0). The objective equals 2(x+y)=6 everywhere on it. The optimal set is a segment and also the whole feasible region.
items.transfer: Maximize x on the same feasible segment. Does the whole segment remain optimal?

items.prompt: Require 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, x ≥ 2 and y ≥ 1. What is the complete optimal set for a zero objective?
options: The whole rectangle
No feasible point, because the region has no area
An infinite line through (2,1)
The single point (2,1), which is also the whole feasible set
items.explanation: The upper and lower bounds force x=2 and y=1. A singleton is a valid nonempty feasible set. Its only point attains the zero objective and constitutes the whole feasible set.
items.transfer: Would changing the objective to 7x-2y change the only feasible point?

items.prompt: A problem already contains x+y ≤ 4. What happens to its feasible set when 2x+2y ≤ 8 is also added?
options: It necessarily becomes smaller because there is another row.
Its geometry is unchanged; the additional row still has its own identity.
It becomes empty because two boundaries are parallel.
Its variables become integers.
items.explanation: Dividing the new inequality by the positive number 2 gives the existing one. The extra condition excludes no additional point. A transparent calculation can still show both authored row identities and their individual slacks.
items.transfer: At (1,1), compare the slacks of the original and doubled rows.

items.prompt: Which added inequality is impossible for every real point?
options: x+y ≤ 100 inside 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 4
items.explanation: The left side of a zero-normal row is always 0. Thus 0 ≤ -1 is false everywhere. The row 0 ≤ 0 is always true and tight; 0 ≤ 4 is always true with slack 4.
items.transfer: Why must a solver distinguish a zero-normal contradiction from a redundant row?

items.prompt: The problem 2x+y ≤ 5, x+2y ≤ 5 in 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 4 maximizes x+y at 10/3. Change the actual upper bound on x to 1. What follows?
options: Only the drawing changes; the optimum stays 10/3.
The new optimum is 3 at (1,2).
The old point (5/3,5/3) remains feasible.
All variables become integers because a bound is 1.
items.explanation: Now x ≤ 1 and x+2y ≤ 5 imply x+y ≤ (5+x)/2 ≤ 3. The point (1,2) satisfies the other inequality and all bounds, so it attains 3. The rectangle is part of the mathematical input.
items.transfer: Identify exactly which new bound excludes the old optimum.

items.prompt: The lab accepts integer coefficients and bounds. Which statement about its variables is correct?
options: Integer coefficients require integer variables.
Only visible grid points are allowed.
Rounding a feasible fractional point upward always preserves feasibility.
The variables are real, so fractional feasible points are allowed.
items.explanation: Integer input tokens make exact rational computation convenient; they do not impose integrality on x or y. In the fractional example, rounding (5/3,5/3) up to (2,2) makes both left sides 6, violating the bound 5.
items.transfer: Why would an integer-programming version be a different optimization problem?

items.prompt: Keep every constraint and rectangle bound fixed, but replace objective 3x+2y with x-y. What must remain unchanged?
options: The feasible set
Every objective value
The complete optimal set
The ordering of vertices by objective value
items.explanation: Feasibility depends on the constraints and bounds, not on the objective. The new objective can reorder vertex values and change which points are optimal. On (0,0), (0,4), (1,3), (5/2,0), its values are 0, -4, -2 and 5/2.
items.transfer: Which of those four vertices maximizes the new objective?
